observations.text: SP, due to power settings not matched to the planned IAS for the flight altitude, did not maintain the calculated cruise airspeed or the planned navigation altitude, with the result of an airspeed excursion of 30 knots and an altitude excursion of 450 feet, both beyond the standard. The IP had to direct and apply part of the power and pitch corrections to re-establish the leg parameters. Study of the cruise power settings per altitude and per leg is required.

SP, due to task sequencing that concentrated all cockpit workload inside the turn, did not monitor heading and altitude while completing the in-flight fuel calculation, with the result of a heading error of 18 degrees and a descent 400 feet below the planned navigation altitude. Recovery to the planned course and altitude was accomplished only after the IP took the aircraft. Basic aircraft control must be protected while the required in-flight procedures are executed.

SP maintained basic aircraft control within the standards required for the Training Section, with airspeed and altitude reaching the limits of 20 knots and 300 feet on two of the legs. Both excursions were recognized and corrected with delay, after the IP's verbal prompts. Marginal performance for the Training Section - earlier recognition of power setting and pitch trends is expected to improve.

SP set the power for the planned IAS on each leg and held the navigation parameters with altitude excursions of 180 feet, airspeed excursions of 12 knots and heading errors of 8 degrees. All deviations were recognized by the SP and corrected in a timely manner, without the IP's intervention. Above end of block MIF achieved.

SP demonstrated accurate and prompt basic aircraft control throughout the route, setting the appropriate power for the planned IAS on every leg and executing the flight altitude changes IAW the Techniques and Procedures Manual. Altitude was held within 100 feet, airspeed within 8 knots and heading within 4 degrees, and the deliberate airspeed changes placed the aircraft over the turning points at the calculated times. Above end of block MIF achieved.

SP flew the navigation legs with exceptional precision, anticipating the power required by each flight altitude change and keeping the aircraft in trim throughout. Deviations did not exceed 50 feet in altitude, 3 knots in airspeed and 2 degrees in heading, while the in-flight fuel calculations against time and distance were completed with no degradation of the scan. Above end of block MIF achieved.

SP, due to a trim technique that was not reapplied after each flight altitude change, did not settle the aircraft on the planned navigation altitude, with the result of repeated excursions exceeding 400 feet and an airspeed 25 knots below the planned IAS. The IP had to intervene on the controls to re-establish the leg parameters.

SP, due to attention captured by the navigation chart while the aircraft state went unmonitored, did not hold the planned heading and navigation altitude between turning points, with the result of a heading error of 20 degrees and a climb 350 feet above the planned altitude. The IP had to direct the corrections and re-establish the aircraft on the planned course. Basic aircraft control has priority over map work during the cruise segment.

SP, due to power settings applied without reference to the planned IAS for the flight altitude and the winds, did not hold the calculated cruise airspeed, with the result of a deviation of 20 knots and an associated altitude excursion of 300 feet, both at the limit of the standard. Recognition was delayed and the corrections were applied only after the IP's verbal prompts.

SP, due to an interrupted instrument cross-check while attention remained on the turning point features, did not monitor the aircraft state through the leg, with the result of a heading error of 10 degrees and an altitude excursion of 300 feet, both at the limit of the standard. The deviations were recognized and corrected with delay, after the IP's verbal prompts. Reconstitution of the scan after each map reference is required.

SP maintained basic aircraft control within the desired standards, holding altitude within 250 feet, airspeed within 15 knots and heading within 9 degrees. Corrections were self-initiated and applied in a timely manner without the IP's intervention, although all three parameters were worked close to their limits. Marginal performance for the Training Section - closer control of altitude during the deliberate airspeed changes is expected to improve.

SP set the appropriate power for the planned IAS on every leg and executed the flight altitude changes IAW the Techniques and Procedures Manual, holding altitude within 120 feet, airspeed within 7 knots and heading within 4 degrees. The in-flight fuel calculations related to time and distance were accurate and were completed without any interruption of the scan. Above end of block MIF achieved.

SP demonstrated exceptional precision in basic aircraft control, anticipating each power and pitch change and keeping deviations to 50 feet in altitude, 3 knots in airspeed and 2 degrees in heading. The deliberate airspeed changes were executed IAW the Techniques and Procedures Manual and placed the aircraft over every turning point at the calculated time, while remaining predictable and comfortable for the wingman. Above end of block MIF achieved.

SP, due to a descent technique in which the rate was not reduced approaching the level-off, did not arrest the descent at the planned navigation altitude, with the result of an excursion of 500 feet below it and an airspeed 30 knots above the planned IAS. The IP had to take the aircraft to re-establish the planned profile.

SP, due to a workload distribution that left the SP flying and transmitting at the same time, did not hold the planned heading and navigation altitude through the turning point, with the result of a heading error of 25 degrees and an altitude excursion of 400 feet. The IP had to direct the recovery to the planned course and altitude, and the calculated time over the following turning point was missed by more than one minute.

SP, due to flight altitude changes flown without the pitch and power values of the Techniques and Procedures Manual, did not level off at the planned navigation altitude, with the result of overshoots reaching 300 feet and an airspeed deviation of 20 knots, both at the limit of the standard. Recognition was delayed and the corrections were completed only after the IP's verbal prompts.

SP, due to lack of awareness of the fuel state during the working phase of the sortie, did not modify the mission profile in time to remain within the fuel restrictions and did not hold the planned cruise IAS while recomputing, with the result of an airspeed deviation of 20 knots and a heading error of 10 degrees, both at the limit of the standard. The profile change and the parameter corrections were made only after the IP's verbal prompts.

SP, due to power corrections applied in steps larger than the leg change required, did not settle the aircraft on the planned cruise IAS after each flight altitude change, with the result of airspeed excursions of 15 knots and altitude excursions of 200 feet. All deviations were recognized and corrected in a timely manner, without the IP's intervention.

SP, due to distraction by a secondary cockpit task during the cruise segment, did not hold the planned heading between turning points, with the result of a track error of 8 degrees and an associated altitude excursion of 220 feet. The errors were recognized by the SP and corrected in a timely manner without the IP's intervention, and the turning point was still crossed within the calculated time.

SP maintained basic aircraft control within the desired standards, holding altitude within 140 feet, airspeed within 9 knots and heading within 5 degrees. Wingman consideration was adequate, although two abrupt power changes during the leg transitions obliged the wingman to work the closure. Marginal performance for the Training Section - smoother power management during the deliberate airspeed changes is expected to improve.

SP flew the entire route with exceptional accuracy, setting the correct power for the planned IAS at each flight altitude and executing all altitude changes IAW the Techniques and Procedures Manual. Deviations did not exceed 50 feet in altitude, 3 knots in airspeed and 2 degrees in heading, the in-flight fuel calculations related to time and distance were accurate throughout, and every airspeed change was flown so as to remain predictable for the wingman. Above end of block MIF achieved.
